name: LSQUIC
workload: 8 GB file download over HTTP/3 on a dedicated 10 Gbit/s link between AMD EPYC 7543 servers, all client/server implementation pairs, 50 repeated runs, measuring goodput (bytes transferred / time)
claimed_speedup: Matched client/server pairs, default config: LSQUIC-LSQUIC 3004 Mbit/s vs quiche-quiche baseline 2506 Mbit/s (~1.2x). With increased UDP receive buffers and arch-tuned compile flags (LSQUIC*/quiche*): LSQUIC-LSQUIC 3882 Mbit/s vs quiche-quiche 2590 Mbit/s (~1.5x). On the newest test CPU (Intel Xeon Gold 6312U), optimized LSQUIC approaches ~5 Gbit/s.
compiler_and_flags: Debian Bullseye, Linux 5.10.0-8-amd64; LSQUIC* variant built with architecture-specific compile flags (exact flags in the paper's companion repo, not fully enumerated in the PDF text)
hardware: AMD EPYC 7543 32-core (primary); also AMD EPYC 7551P, Intel Xeon D-1518, Intel Xeon E5-1650, Intel Xeon Gold 6312U (cross-CPU comparison in Fig. 9)
tradeoffs: C API (less ergonomic than Rust quiche); goodput is highly sensitive to UDP buffer sizing, CPU generation, and cipher (LSQUIC drops to 30-70% of Cubic goodput when misconfigured with BBR); cross-implementation pairing is asymmetric -- quiche-server+LSQUIC-client reaches 2556 Mbit/s but LSQUIC-server+quiche-client only 1186 Mbit/s, more than 2x lower, so the win is config/direction dependent, not a uniform speedup
caveats: Paper's baseline measurements are from ~January 2023 software versions of both libraries; QUIC implementations change quickly so current relative standing may differ. quiche itself is one of the four named category baselines, so this is evidence for a KNOWN_LIST project (LSQUIC) beating a baseline, not a new discovery.
found_via: arXiv search 'QUIC implementations performance comparison goodput' -> 'QUIC on the Highway: Evaluating Performance on High-rate Links' (Jaeger, Zirngibl, Kempf, Ploch, Carle; IFIP Networking 2023), code at github.com/tumi8/quic-10g-paper

name: Unbound
workload: DNS Shotgun load test measuring maximum sustained queries answered per second over a 120s window, per transport (UDP, DoT, DoH-GET, DoH-POST), against a fixed real-world query trace, for Knot Resolver 6.2.0/5.7.6, Unbound 1.24.2, and BIND 9.20.18/9.21.17
claimed_speedup: Unbound 1.24.2 sustains >300K UDP queries/s vs BIND 9.20.18's 225K and BIND 9.21.17's 125K (roughly 1.3-2.4x depending on BIND version); on DoT/DoH, Unbound and Knot Resolver 5.7.6 are tied at 110K/90K/90K, both ahead of BIND9's 100K/80K/80K (9.20.18) and 70K/60K/50K (9.21.17)
hardware: Dell PowerEdge R6515, AMD EPYC 7702P underclocked to 1.5 GHz, 8x8GB DDR4, Intel X710 10GbE; 6 worker processes
tradeoffs: Recursive resolver, not a stub-resolver library like c-ares -- different deployment role. Absolute numbers are CPU-throttled and the page itself cautions 'absolute values shown in the graphs are not directly comparable' across hardware/runs, so treat as relative ranking evidence, not portable throughput figures.
caveats: Benchmark is run and published by the competing Knot Resolver project (CZ.NIC) using their own open-source DNS Shotgun tool (github.com/CZ-NIC/shotgun), but it directly measures third-party BIND9 and Unbound with stated versions and hardware, so treated as an independent shootout rather than a first-party claim. Unbound is already on KNOWN_LIST; reported here only as is_evidence_for_known against BIND9, a widely used incumbent not on the baseline list.
found_via: Orchestrator hint 'DNS resolver benchmark blog series (e.g. NLnet Labs, CZ.NIC, ISC)' -> gh api repos/CZ-NIC/knot-resolver -> WebFetch https://www.knot-resolver.cz/benchmark/
